title: The Hidden Cost of Free Shipping
paras: For online retailers, free shipping has become less a perk than an expectation. Surveys consistently find that unexpected delivery charges are the leading reason shoppers abandon their digital carts, and many firms have responded by absorbing shipping costs entirely. The logic seems sound: if a fee drives customers away, removing it should raise sales enough to cover the expense.

Yet the arithmetic is rarely so kind. Shipping costs do not disappear when a retailer stops charging for them; they migrate into higher product prices, into thinner margins, or into minimum order thresholds that quietly push customers to buy more than they intended. Retailers that rely on thresholds often discover that the extra items customers add are disproportionately low-margin goods, chosen precisely because they are cheap enough to carry an order across the line. Worse, generous free shipping encourages "bracketing," the practice of ordering several sizes or colors of an item and returning all but one, which multiplies handling and restocking costs.

None of this means that free shipping is a mistake. For retailers with high average order values or a base of loyal repeat customers, the policy can pay for itself by turning occasional purchases into habits. The error lies in treating free shipping as a universal remedy rather than as a tool whose value depends on a particular firm's mix of products and customers.

questions.stem: The primary purpose of the passage is to
choices: explain why shoppers abandon online carts when they encounter delivery charges
argue that the value of free shipping depends on a retailer's specific circumstances
recommend that online retailers stop offering free shipping to their customers
compare the profitability of minimum order thresholds with that of flat shipping fees
describe how retailers can reduce the handling costs created by product returns
questions.explanation: Paragraph 1 states the case for free shipping, paragraph 2 lists its hidden costs, and paragraph 3 concludes that the policy is not a mistake but "a tool whose value depends on a particular firm's mix of products and customers." That balanced, conditional claim is (B). (C) contradicts "None of this means that free shipping is a mistake." (A), (D) and (E) are details or topics the passage never develops as its main point.

questions.stem: According to the passage, bracketing raises a retailer's costs because it
choices: leads customers to add low-margin items to their orders
requires the retailer to raise the listed prices of its products
increases the number of items that must be handled and restocked after being returned
discourages loyal customers from making repeat purchases
causes shoppers to abandon their carts before completing a purchase
questions.explanation: Paragraph 2 defines bracketing as ordering several sizes or colors "and returning all but one, which multiplies handling and restocking costs." That is (C). (A) describes the effect of minimum order thresholds, not bracketing. (B), (D) and (E) are not linked to bracketing anywhere in the passage.

questions.stem: The author would most likely agree with which of the following statements about a retailer whose customers place small orders and rarely return to buy again?
choices: It should offer free shipping only on orders that include low-margin goods.
It is likely to recover the cost of free shipping through increased customer loyalty.
It would gain more from free shipping than a retailer with high average order values.
It cannot be harmed by bracketing because its customers buy few items.
It should be cautious about assuming that unconditional free shipping will pay for itself.
questions.explanation: Paragraph 3 says free shipping "can pay for itself" for retailers "with high average order values or a base of loyal repeat customers." A retailer with small orders and one-time buyers has neither advantage, so the author would urge caution, as in (E). (B) and (C) reverse the passage's logic. (A) and (D) are unsupported: bracketing depends on returns, not on order size.

title: How Salmon Find Home
paras: Pacific salmon begin life in freshwater streams, migrate to the ocean as juveniles, and spend several years feeding hundreds or even thousands of kilometers from where they hatched. When they mature, most return not merely to the right river but to the very tributary of their birth, where they spawn and die. How they accomplish this feat puzzled biologists for much of the twentieth century.

The first persuasive answer came from studies of smell. In the 1950s, researchers proposed that young salmon memorize, or imprint on, the distinctive chemical signature of their home stream before leaving it. Salmon whose nasal openings were plugged chose between river branches no better than chance, while intact fish reliably selected their natal branch. In a later series of experiments, juvenile salmon exposed to a synthetic chemical called morpholine were, as adults, drawn to streams that had been scented with that same chemical, even though it was foreign to their actual birthplace.

Smell, however, cannot explain the open-ocean portion of the journey, where stream odors are diluted beyond detection. A growing body of evidence suggests that salmon also imprint on the Earth's magnetic field at the point where their river meets the sea. Sockeye salmon returning to British Columbia's Fraser River must pass Vancouver Island by either a northern or a southern route. Over several decades, the proportion of fish using each route shifted in step with slow drift in the planet's magnetic field: the salmon favored whichever route brought them to a field that more closely matched the one they had experienced as juveniles.

The two mechanisms are best understood as complementary rather than competing. Magnetic cues appear to bring salmon to the general stretch of coastline, and smell then guides them through the final branching network of streams. Neither system is infallible. Salmon raised in hatcheries stray into the wrong rivers far more often than wild fish do, a finding that suggests imprinting depends on environmental conditions that hatcheries do not fully reproduce.

questions.stem: Which of the following best states the main idea of the passage?
choices: Salmon rely mainly on magnetic cues because stream odors are too weak to detect.
Hatchery-raised salmon should be released only into streams scented with morpholine.
Salmon appear to combine magnetic and chemical cues to find their home streams.
Biologists have abandoned the theory that salmon navigate by smell.
The magnetic field near the Fraser River has changed more rapidly than expected.
questions.explanation: Paragraphs 2 and 3 present smell and magnetism, and paragraph 4 concludes that "the two mechanisms are best understood as complementary rather than competing." That is (C). (A) and (D) ignore that smell still guides the "final branching network of streams." (B) is never proposed, and (E) is a narrow detail.

questions.stem: According to the passage, the morpholine experiments showed that salmon
choices: are attracted as adults to a chemical they were exposed to as juveniles
cannot detect synthetic chemicals that are foreign to their birthplace
navigate the open ocean by following chemical trails
lose the ability to imprint when raised in hatcheries
prefer streams whose magnetic field matches that of their birthplace
questions.explanation: Paragraph 2 reports that juveniles "exposed to a synthetic chemical called morpholine were, as adults, drawn to streams that had been scented with that same chemical." That is (A). (B) contradicts the result. (C) contradicts paragraph 3's statement that odors are undetectable in the open ocean. (D) and (E) concern other findings.

questions.stem: The author discusses the two routes around Vancouver Island primarily in order to
choices: show that sockeye salmon are less reliable navigators than other salmon
suggest that the southern route is more dangerous than the northern one
explain why smell cannot guide salmon in the open ocean
provide evidence that the magnetic field influences salmon migration
argue that hatchery fish choose routes differently from wild fish
questions.explanation: In paragraph 3, the route proportions "shifted in step with slow drift in the planet's magnetic field," with fish favoring the route whose field matched their juvenile experience. The example is evidence for magnetic imprinting, (D). (C) is stated in the paragraph's first sentence, before the example. (A), (B) and (E) are not discussed.

questions.stem: It can be inferred from the passage that the higher straying rate of hatchery salmon
choices: proves that hatchery salmon cannot detect the magnetic field
indicates that the conditions under which salmon are reared may affect how well they imprint
shows that smell plays no role in the final stage of migration
results from hatchery fish being exposed to morpholine
suggests that wild salmon rely exclusively on magnetic cues
questions.explanation: Paragraph 4 says the straying "suggests imprinting depends on environmental conditions that hatcheries do not fully reproduce." So rearing conditions may affect imprinting, (B). (A) overstates: "proves" and the specific claim about magnetism are unsupported. (C) and (E) contradict the complementary model. (D) is not mentioned.

title: Pricing on Two Sides
paras: Many businesses sell to two distinct groups whose demand is linked: a credit card network serves both cardholders and merchants, and a video game console serves both players and game developers. Such platforms frequently charge one group little or nothing, or even pay it to participate. Card networks reward cardholders with cash back while collecting fees from merchants; console makers have often sold hardware below cost while collecting royalties from developers.

Judged by the standards of ordinary markets, these practices look irrational or predatory, since one side is priced below the cost of serving it. But on a two-sided platform, the value each group derives depends on how many members of the other group participate. A network that charged cardholders heavily would attract few of them, and merchants would then have little reason to accept its cards. Subsidizing the side whose presence most attracts the other can therefore maximize the platform's total profit. Which side deserves the subsidy is not fixed: whereas console makers subsidized players, early makers of personal computer operating systems courted developers with free programming tools and charged users instead.

Regulators who examine each side's prices in isolation thus risk mistaking a sensible pricing structure for an attempt to drive out rivals. Yet the two-sided logic should not become a blanket defense. Because subsidies can make a large platform difficult to dislodge, the same pricing that builds a network can also be used to entrench one.

questions.stem: The author mentions early makers of personal computer operating systems primarily in order to
choices: show that the side of a platform that receives a subsidy varies across markets
suggest that software developers are more price-sensitive than players
give an example of pricing that regulators correctly identified as predatory
argue that operating system makers earned less than console makers
illustrate how subsidies can make a large platform difficult to dislodge
questions.explanation: Paragraph 2 says "Which side deserves the subsidy is not fixed" and contrasts console makers, who subsidized players, with operating system makers, who subsidized developers. The example shows variation, (A). (B) and (D) are not claimed. (C) and (E) refer to regulation and entrenchment, which are discussed in paragraph 3, not in connection with this example.

questions.stem: It can be inferred that the "standards of ordinary markets" mentioned in the passage would evaluate a platform's pricing by
choices: comparing the platform's total profit with that of its rivals
estimating how many members of each group the platform attracts
comparing the price charged to each group with the cost of serving that group alone
determining which group's presence most attracts the other group
measuring how difficult it would be for a rival to displace the platform
questions.explanation: Paragraph 2 says that by ordinary standards these practices look predatory "since one side is priced below the cost of serving it," and paragraph 3 refers to regulators who "examine each side's prices in isolation." So the ordinary test compares each side's price with its own cost, (C). (B) and (D) describe the two-sided reasoning that the ordinary test ignores. (A) and (E) are not part of that test.

questions.stem: The author's attitude toward the two-sided explanation of platform pricing can best be described as
choices: dismissive, because it excuses predatory conduct
neutral, because the author offers no evaluation of it
uncritical, because the author sees no limits to its application
hostile, because it has misled regulators
generally favorable but mindful of its potential for misuse
questions.explanation: The author endorses the logic, saying subsidies "can therefore maximize the platform's total profit" and warning that isolated analysis risks misjudging "a sensible pricing structure." But paragraph 3 adds that it "should not become a blanket defense" because subsidies can entrench a platform. That qualified approval is (E). (A) and (D) are too negative; (B) ignores the clear stance; (C) ignores the caveat.

title: The Power of the Default
paras: For decades, employees who wished to join a workplace retirement plan had to take action: fill out a form, choose a contribution rate, and select investments. Many never did. Even when employers offered generous matching contributions, which amount to free money, participation among new workers often hovered below half. Economists who assumed that people reliably pursue their own financial interests found these numbers puzzling, since declining a match is equivalent to refusing part of one's salary. Surveys added to the mystery: most nonparticipants said they intended to join the plan soon, yet months later many still had not done so.

The puzzle became sharper when some firms reversed the default, enrolling every new employee automatically while allowing anyone to withdraw. In one widely studied company, participation among new hires rose from under 50 percent to more than 85 percent, although the plan's benefits had not changed at all. Behavioral economists explain the effect through several tendencies: inertia, by which people stick with whatever requires no action; procrastination, by which they postpone decisions that seem complicated; and implied endorsement, by which employees read the default as a recommendation from their employer.

Yet automatic enrollment produced a less celebrated result as well. Most enrolled workers remained at the default contribution rate, which in many plans was set at a modest 3 percent of salary, and in a conservative default investment fund. Some employees who, under the old system, would have deliberately chosen to save 6 or 8 percent instead drifted into the lower default. For them, a policy designed to raise saving reduced it.

The lesson is not that defaults are harmful but that they are never neutral. Whatever option a planner designates as the default will be adopted by large numbers of people who do not consider the alternatives, so the choice of default is itself a consequential decision. Some plans have responded by pairing automatic enrollment with automatic escalation, raising contributions a little each year unless the employee objects, an approach that uses the same inertia to push saving upward.

questions.stem: The passage is primarily concerned with
choices: explaining why employees fail to take advantage of employer matching contributions
arguing that automatic enrollment should be replaced by automatic escalation
showing that defaults strongly shape behavior, so the choice of default carries real consequences
criticizing behavioral economists for overstating the effects of inertia
comparing the investment returns of conservative and aggressive retirement funds
questions.explanation: The passage shows that switching the default raised participation (paragraph 2), notes an unintended effect on contribution rates (paragraph 3), and concludes that defaults "are never neutral" and that "the choice of default is itself a consequential decision." That is (C). (A) covers only paragraph 1. (B) misreads escalation as a replacement; it is paired with enrollment. (D) and (E) are not argued.

questions.stem: Which of the following is cited in the passage as a reason that automatic enrollment raises participation?
choices: Employees interpret the default as a recommendation from their employer.
Automatic enrollment increases the size of employer matching contributions.
Employees who are enrolled automatically receive higher investment returns.
Employers require automatically enrolled workers to remain in the plan.
Automatic enrollment removes the option to choose a contribution rate.
questions.explanation: Paragraph 2 lists "implied endorsement, by which employees read the default as a recommendation from their employer." That is (A). (B) contradicts "the plan's benefits had not changed at all." (D) contradicts "allowing anyone to withdraw." (C) and (E) are not stated.

questions.stem: It can be inferred from the passage that automatic enrollment reduced saving among employees who
choices: would never have joined the plan under the old system
withdrew from the plan soon after being enrolled
chose a conservative investment fund on their own initiative
received the largest employer matching contributions
would have actively selected a contribution rate above the default
questions.explanation: Paragraph 3 says that some employees "who, under the old system, would have deliberately chosen to save 6 or 8 percent instead drifted into the lower default." Their saving fell, so (E). For those in (A), enrollment raised saving from zero. (B), (C) and (D) are not linked to reduced saving in the passage.

questions.stem: Which of the following situations is most closely analogous to the unintended result described in the third paragraph?
choices: A gym that charges a high cancellation fee finds that few members cancel their memberships.
A city that switches organ donation to an opt-out system, with a default covering only a few organs, finds that some people who would have pledged all organs now pledge fewer.
A company that stops offering a cafeteria discount finds that employees bring lunch from home.
A school that requires students to choose an elective finds that many delay their decision until the deadline.
A library that extends its hours finds that more patrons visit in the evening.
questions.explanation: Paragraph 3 describes a default that raises overall participation but pulls some people who would have chosen more down to a modest default level. In (B), opt-out raises participation while some who would have chosen a fuller commitment settle at the limited default. (D) illustrates procrastination only. (A), (C) and (E) involve fees, prices or hours, not a default that lowers some people's chosen level.

title: Japanese Prints and European Painting
paras: After Japan reopened to Western trade in the 1850s, woodblock prints of the ukiyo-e school began to circulate in Paris, at first as curiosities and soon as prized collectibles. Monet covered the walls of his dining room with them, and Degas and Van Gogh studied them closely. The standard account of this episode, known as Japonisme, holds that the prints introduced European painters to a set of new pictorial devices: flat areas of unmodulated color, asymmetrical compositions, figures abruptly cropped by the frame, and steep, high vantage points.

This account captures the enthusiasm of the period but overstates its novelty. Several of these devices were already emerging in European art. Cropped, off-center figures appeared in the work of painters who studied the accidental framing of early photographs, and a reaction against the smooth, sculptural modeling taught in the academies had already pushed some artists toward flatter color. What the prints supplied was less a new vocabulary than a precedent: a mature and admired tradition in which such devices were conventions rather than errors. An artist accused of clumsy drawing could point to Hiroshige or Hokusai as proof that the same choices could produce masterpieces.

Van Gogh's practice illustrates the point. When he painted copies of Hiroshige prints, he did not reproduce their colors faithfully but intensified them into the saturated yellows and greens of his own palette. He treated the prints not as models to be imitated but as permission to pursue what he had already begun.

questions.stem: The author's main point is that Japanese prints
choices: were valued in Paris chiefly as curiosities rather than as works of art
introduced photography-inspired cropping to European painting
had less influence on Van Gogh than on Monet and Degas
lent legitimacy to artistic tendencies that were already developing in Europe
were imitated faithfully by most of the European painters who collected them
questions.explanation: Paragraph 2 argues that the standard account "overstates its novelty" and that the prints supplied "less a new vocabulary than a precedent" for devices "already emerging in European art." Paragraph 3 calls them "permission." That is (D). (B) reverses the source of cropping. (E) contradicts the Van Gogh example. (A) and (C) are unsupported.

questions.stem: According to the passage, the standard account of Japonisme credits Japanese prints with introducing European painters to
choices: smooth, sculptural modeling of figures
steep, high vantage points
the saturated yellows and greens of Van Gogh's palette
the accidental framing of early photographs
faithful reproduction of an original's colors
questions.explanation: Paragraph 1 lists the devices attributed to the prints: "flat areas of unmodulated color, asymmetrical compositions, figures abruptly cropped by the frame, and steep, high vantage points." That includes (B). (A) is the academic style artists reacted against. (C) is Van Gogh's own palette, and (D) is a European source of cropping. (E) is what Van Gogh did not do.

questions.stem: The author describes Van Gogh's alteration of Hiroshige's colors in order to
choices: support the claim that painters used the prints as encouragement rather than as templates
show that Van Gogh misunderstood the conventions of Japanese printmaking
argue that Van Gogh was the most original painter influenced by Japonisme
explain why Japanese prints became prized collectibles in Paris
suggest that Hiroshige's colors were too muted for European tastes
questions.explanation: Paragraph 3 opens with "Van Gogh's practice illustrates the point" and ends by saying he treated the prints "not as models to be imitated but as permission." The detail about intensified colors supports the thesis that prints served as precedent, (A). (B), (C), (D) and (E) all go beyond what the passage claims.

title: The Wood Wide Web Reconsidered
paras: Beneath most forests lies a dense web of mycorrhizal fungi, whose threadlike hyphae colonize tree roots and trade soil nutrients for sugars the trees produce. Because a single fungus can colonize several trees at once, these networks physically connect neighboring plants. In recent years, popular books and documentaries have described the network as a kind of forest internet through which large "mother trees" feed their seedlings and send chemical warnings of insect attack.

The evidence for this picture is thinner than its popularity suggests. Field studies using labeled carbon have shown that carbon can pass from one tree to another, but few have ruled out alternative routes, such as diffusion through soil or uptake from decaying roots, so it is often unclear that the fungus carried the carbon at all. The quantities detected are usually small. Moreover, transfer does not imply benefit: the fungus is an organism with its own interests, and it may shuttle carbon to wherever it gains the most, not to wherever a seedling needs it most. Studies of seedling growth near established trees are similarly mixed, with roughly as many reporting neutral or negative effects as positive ones.

None of this shows that the networks are unimportant. It shows that the story of cooperative forests has outrun the data. Experiments that sever fungal connections while blocking soil pathways, and that track seedling survival over many years, would do more to settle the question than further eloquent narratives.

questions.stem: The author's attitude toward the popular view of mycorrhizal networks is best described as
choices: enthusiastic endorsement
measured skepticism
complete indifference
outright hostility
reluctant acceptance
questions.explanation: Paragraph 2 says the evidence "is thinner than its popularity suggests," yet paragraph 3 notes "None of this shows that the networks are unimportant" and calls for better experiments. The author doubts the popular story without rejecting the networks, so (B). (D) is too strong given that concession. (A) and (E) imply agreement; (C) ignores the clear stance.

questions.stem: Which of the following findings would the author most likely regard as the strongest support for the claim that trees feed seedlings through fungal networks?
choices: Carbon labeled in a mature tree is later detected in the soil surrounding nearby seedlings.
Seedlings growing near large trees are, on average, taller than seedlings growing in open ground.
Hyphae from a single fungus are found attached to the roots of several neighboring trees.
With soil pathways blocked, seedlings with intact fungal links to a mature tree gain more labeled carbon and survive longer than seedlings whose links are cut.
Popular accounts of mother trees have been widely accepted by forest managers.
questions.explanation: Paragraph 2 objects that studies rarely rule out soil routes and that transfer may not benefit seedlings; paragraph 3 calls for experiments "that sever fungal connections while blocking soil pathways" and track survival. (D) describes exactly that design with a positive result. (A) does not exclude soil routes. (B) could have other causes. (C) shows connection, not transfer or benefit. (E) is not evidence.

questions.stem: The author's remark that the fungus "is an organism with its own interests" serves primarily to
choices: suggest that observed carbon transfer need not reflect cooperation among trees
argue that mycorrhizal fungi harm the trees they colonize
explain why the quantities of carbon detected are usually small
show that the fungus, rather than soil diffusion, carries most of the carbon
propose that fungi deliberately warn trees of insect attack
questions.explanation: In paragraph 2 the remark follows "transfer does not imply benefit" and explains that the fungus may move carbon "to wherever it gains the most, not to wherever a seedling needs it most." The point is that transfer may serve the fungus, not a cooperative purpose among trees, (A). (B) overstates. (C) and (D) concern separate points. (E) restates the popular claim the author questions.

title: When Cost Accounting Misleads
paras: Traditional cost accounting assigns a factory's overhead, the costs of supervision, setups, engineering, and materials handling, to products in proportion to the direct labor hours each product consumes. When overhead was a small share of total cost and labor a large one, this shortcut introduced little error. In many modern plants the proportions have reversed: automation has shrunk direct labor while overhead has swollen, so the basis of allocation bears little relation to what actually generates the costs being allocated.

The distortion is systematic. A low-volume specialty product may require as many machine setups, engineering changes, and quality inspections as a high-volume standard product, yet it absorbs only a sliver of overhead because it uses few labor hours. Labor-based systems therefore tend to overstate the cost of standard products and understate the cost of specialty ones. Managers relying on these figures may cut prices on specialty items they believe to be lucrative while abandoning standard lines they believe to be marginal.

Activity-based costing, or ABC, attempts to correct the problem by tracing overhead to the activities that cause it and assigning each activity's cost according to how heavily each product uses it. Firms that adopted ABC in the 1980s and 1990s sometimes found that their most celebrated specialty lines were losing money. Even so, adoption has remained limited. Detailed ABC systems are expensive to build and to update, the choice of cost drivers involves judgment that invites dispute, and managers whose products look worse under the new figures have every reason to question them.

These obstacles are real, but they partly reflect a misunderstanding of what ABC is for. Its chief value lies less in producing precise unit costs than in forcing managers to ask what drives their costs at all. A rough model built around a handful of major activities may therefore be more useful than an elaborate one that collapses under the burden of its own maintenance.

questions.stem: The primary purpose of the passage is to
choices: trace the history of cost accounting from the 1980s to the present
argue that firms should abandon specialty products in favor of standard ones
explain a flaw in traditional costing and assess an alternative and its proper use
demonstrate that activity-based costing produces more precise unit costs than any other method
criticize managers for resisting changes in accounting methods
questions.explanation: Paragraphs 1 and 2 explain the flaw in labor-based allocation; paragraph 3 introduces ABC and obstacles to adoption; paragraph 4 says ABC's "chief value lies less in producing precise unit costs than in forcing managers to ask what drives their costs." (C) covers all of this. (D) contradicts paragraph 4. (A), (B) and (E) are too narrow or unsupported.

questions.stem: According to the passage, labor-based costing systems understate the cost of low-volume specialty products because such products
choices: require fewer machine setups than standard products
use few labor hours yet consume a large share of overhead-generating activities
are usually priced below the cost of producing them
are produced in plants that rely heavily on direct labor
are excluded from the allocation of overhead costs
questions.explanation: Paragraph 2 says a specialty product "may require as many machine setups, engineering changes, and quality inspections" as a standard one, "yet it absorbs only a sliver of overhead because it uses few labor hours." That is (B). (A) contradicts this. (C) is a possible consequence, not the cause. (D) and (E) are unsupported.

questions.stem: It can be inferred from the passage that a factory whose overhead is a small fraction of its total costs and whose direct labor is a large fraction would
choices: gain relatively little from switching to activity-based costing
be unable to identify which of its products are profitable
overstate the cost of its specialty products
find that its cost drivers are especially easy to dispute
need an unusually elaborate activity-based costing model
questions.explanation: Paragraph 1 states that "When overhead was a small share of total cost and labor a large one, this shortcut introduced little error." If the traditional method is already fairly accurate in such a factory, ABC would offer little improvement, (A). (B) and (C) contradict that low error. (D) and (E) are not supported.

questions.stem: Which of the following best describes the organization of the passage?
choices: A theory is proposed, tested against evidence, and finally rejected.
Two accounting methods are compared, and the older one is shown to be superior.
A historical trend is described, its causes are debated, and a prediction is made.
A common practice is criticized, and several alternatives are ranked by their costs.
A problem with a conventional practice is explained, a remedy is described along with obstacles to its use, and a view of the remedy's real value is offered.
questions.explanation: Paragraphs 1 and 2 explain the problem with labor-based allocation, paragraph 3 presents ABC and the obstacles to adopting it, and paragraph 4 argues that its value lies in prompting questions about cost drivers. That sequence is (E). (A) and (B) misstate the stance; no theory is rejected and the older method is not favored. (C) omits the remedy. (D) wrongly says several alternatives are ranked.

title: Famine Amid Plenty
paras: It seems self-evident that famines occur when there is not enough food. The economist Amartya Sen challenged this assumption in his analysis of the Bengal famine of 1943, in which perhaps three million people died. Sen argued that the total supply of rice available in Bengal that year was not dramatically lower than in earlier years that had seen no famine. What collapsed was not food but entitlement: the ability of particular groups to command food through their wages, crops, or other resources. Wartime spending in Calcutta and speculative hoarding drove rice prices sharply upward, while the wages of rural laborers barely moved. Landless workers, fishermen, and artisans found that their earnings could no longer buy enough to eat, even as rice remained for sale in local markets.

The entitlement approach carries a clear policy implication. If famine is a failure of purchasing power, then relief may be better delivered through public employment or cash payments than through shipments of grain alone.

Some historians have since argued that Sen underestimated the 1943 shortfall, and that availability mattered more than he allowed. The objection, even if correct, leaves the core of his framework intact. A decline in supply cannot by itself explain why a famine kills laborers and fishermen in great numbers while sparing landowners and city clerks. Explaining who starves requires attention to entitlements, whatever the size of the harvest.

questions.stem: According to the passage, many rural laborers in Bengal were unable to obtain enough food in 1943 because
choices: rice was no longer sold in local markets
the government confiscated their crops for wartime use
the rice harvest was the smallest in Bengal's history
they moved to Calcutta in search of employment
their wages failed to keep pace with rising rice prices
questions.explanation: Paragraph 1 states that rice prices rose sharply "while the wages of rural laborers barely moved," so their earnings "could no longer buy enough to eat, even as rice remained for sale in local markets." That is (E). (A) contradicts the final clause. (C) contradicts Sen's claim that supply was not dramatically lower. (B) and (D) are not mentioned.

questions.stem: The author would most likely respond to the historians mentioned in the third paragraph by arguing that
choices: their estimates of the 1943 rice supply are certainly mistaken
food availability played no role in the Bengal famine
Sen's policy recommendations should be abandoned if their estimates are correct
a larger shortfall would still not account for which groups suffered most
landowners suffered as severely as laborers during the famine
questions.explanation: The author grants that the objection may be "correct" but says it "leaves the core of his framework intact" because supply "cannot by itself explain why a famine kills laborers and fishermen in great numbers while sparing landowners." That is (D). (A) contradicts "even if correct." (B) overstates; the author does not deny any role for availability. (C) and (E) contradict the passage.

questions.stem: Which of the following relief measures would be most consistent with the entitlement approach as described in the passage?
choices: Paying wages to affected laborers for work on public construction projects
Banning the export of rice from the affected region
Importing additional grain to be stored in government warehouses
Encouraging affected laborers to move to cities
Increasing the land held by large landowners
questions.explanation: Paragraph 2 says that if famine is "a failure of purchasing power," relief may be better delivered "through public employment or cash payments than through shipments of grain alone." Paying wages for public works restores purchasing power, (A). (B) and (C) address supply rather than entitlements. (D) and (E) are not suggested and do not directly restore the laborers' command over food.

title: Homer and the Oral Formula
paras: Readers of the Iliad and the Odyssey have long noticed their repeated phrases: Achilles is "swift-footed," dawn is "rosy-fingered," the sea is "wine-dark." In the 1920s and 1930s the American scholar Milman Parry showed that these epithets form a remarkably economical system. For a given character and a given position in the hexameter line, there is usually just one formula that fits, a property Parry called thrift. Achilles is "swift-footed" in some passages where he is sitting still, because the phrase fills the metrical slot, not because it suits the moment.

Parry concluded that such a system could not be the invention of a single author writing at leisure. It was the accumulated toolkit of generations of illiterate poets who composed while they performed, drawing on ready-made phrases to keep pace with the meter. To test this idea, Parry and his student Albert Lord recorded singers in Yugoslavia who still performed long heroic songs without writing, and they found the same reliance on formulas. The Homeric poems, on this view, belong to a tradition rather than to a solitary genius.

The theory transformed the field, but in its stronger forms it overreached. If formulas were chosen purely for meter, they could carry no pointed meaning, yet later scholars have identified many passages where a standard epithet acquires irony or pathos from its context. More tellingly, the Yugoslav songs, however long, rarely display the large-scale architecture of the Iliad, whose episodes echo and answer one another across thousands of lines. Some scholars have suggested that the poems took shape when a singer dictated to a scribe, a process slow enough to permit a degree of planning that live performance does not.
Parry was right about the medium in which Homer worked. His error, or rather that of his more zealous followers, was to assume that the medium dictated everything the poet could achieve within it.

questions.stem: Which of the following best expresses the main idea of the passage?
choices: Parry's discovery of formulaic thrift proves that Homer could not have composed with any artistic intent.
The Yugoslav singers recorded by Parry and Lord were more skilled than the poet of the Iliad.
Homer composed the Iliad in writing, so Parry's oral theory should be discarded.
Parry correctly identified Homer's oral, formulaic medium, but the strong claim that this medium ruled out deliberate artistry goes too far.
Homeric epithets were chosen for their meaning rather than for their metrical fit.
questions.explanation: Paragraphs 1 and 2 present Parry's findings, paragraph 3 says the theory "in its stronger forms it overreached," and paragraph 4 says Parry "was right about the medium" but followers wrongly assumed "the medium dictated everything." That is (D). (A) is the overreach the author rejects. (C) and (E) reject Parry's sound findings. (B) is unsupported.

questions.stem: According to the passage, the property Parry called "thrift" refers to the fact that
choices: Homeric poets used as few words as possible in each line
for a given character and metrical position there is usually only one fitting formula
the same epithet is applied to many different characters
Yugoslav singers performed their songs without writing
the Iliad's episodes echo one another across thousands of lines
questions.explanation: Paragraph 1 states: "For a given character and a given position in the hexameter line, there is usually just one formula that fits, a property Parry called thrift." That is (B). (A) and (C) distort the idea. (D) and (E) are different points from paragraphs 2 and 3.

questions.stem: The author mentions that the Yugoslav songs "rarely display the large-scale architecture of the Iliad" in order to
choices: suggest that the Homeric poems may have been shaped by conditions beyond ordinary live performance
show that Parry and Lord recorded their singers incorrectly
argue that oral composition always produces shorter works than written composition
prove that Homer was not familiar with formulaic composition
explain why standard epithets can acquire irony from their context
questions.explanation: In paragraph 3 the contrast is introduced with "More tellingly" and followed by the suggestion that the poems were dictated to a scribe, "a process slow enough to permit a degree of planning that live performance does not." So the point is that something beyond ordinary performance may explain Homer's unity, (A). (C) overgeneralizes; the songs are called "long." (D) contradicts the author's acceptance of the medium. (B) and (E) are not the purpose.

questions.stem: The author's attitude toward Milman Parry's work is best described as
choices: contemptuous of its methods and conclusions
uncritically admiring of all its claims
respectful of its central insight while critical of an overextension of it
indifferent to its influence on later scholarship
puzzled by its continuing popularity
questions.explanation: The author says the theory "transformed the field" and that Parry "was right about the medium," yet criticizes the "stronger forms" that "overreached," attributing the error mainly to "his more zealous followers." That combination is (C). (A) and (B) are one-sided. (D) and (E) do not match the engaged evaluation.

title: The Island Rule
paras: Islands have long served as natural laboratories for evolution, and few island patterns are as striking as changes in body size. Elephants that colonized Mediterranean islands such as Sicily and Malta evolved into dwarfs, some little more than a meter tall at the shoulder; hippopotamuses on Cyprus and Crete shrank as well. Meanwhile, some rodents on islands evolved into giants many times the mass of their mainland relatives. The generalization that large mammals tend to dwarf on islands while small ones tend toward gigantism has come to be called the island rule.

Several explanations have been offered. Limited food on small islands may favor large animals that need less to survive. The absence of predators may release small animals from the need to stay small enough to hide, allowing larger bodies that are advantageous in competition or in surviving lean seasons. A third account holds that island species converge on an intermediate body size that is optimal for a mammal in an environment with few competitors and few predators, so that dwarfing and gigantism are two expressions of a single tendency.

The changes can be fast. Red deer stranded on the island of Jersey during a period of high sea levels appear to have shrunk to roughly a sixth of their ancestral mass within about six thousand years, a pace implying strong selection.

Recent statistical surveys, however, have found that the rule holds less consistently than textbooks imply. Many island lineages show no clear trend, and the effect is strongest on small, remote islands. In some groups, the pattern depends not on the animal's own size but on its circumstances: island carnivores, for instance, tend to change size in line with the prey available to them. The island rule is therefore better understood as a statistical tendency than as a law. It emerges when particular pressures, such as scarce resources, missing predators, and altered prey, act together, and its predictive value lies in identifying which of those pressures operate on a given island.

questions.stem: The passage is primarily concerned with
choices: describing a pattern of body-size change on islands, its proposed explanations, and limits on its generality
proving that island dwarfing occurs more rapidly than island gigantism
arguing that the absence of predators is the sole cause of body-size change on islands
explaining why Mediterranean elephants became extinct
comparing body-size changes in island carnivores with those in island rodents
questions.explanation: Paragraph 1 describes the island rule, paragraph 2 gives three explanations, paragraph 3 notes the speed of change, and paragraph 4 qualifies the rule as "a statistical tendency" rather than a law. That is (A). (C) contradicts the multiple pressures in paragraph 4. (B), (D) and (E) are unsupported or too narrow.

questions.stem: Based on the passage, a mid-sized carnivore that colonized an island on which the only available prey were much smaller than its mainland prey would most likely
choices: grow larger, because island species tend toward gigantism
remain the same size, because carnivores do not follow the island rule
become smaller, because island carnivores tend to change size in line with available prey
grow larger, because the absence of predators releases it from the need to hide
become extinct, because islands cannot support carnivores
questions.explanation: Paragraph 4 says that "island carnivores, for instance, tend to change size in line with the prey available to them." With much smaller prey, the carnivore would be expected to shrink, (C). (A) and (D) apply rules to the animal's own size or predator release, which the passage says do not govern carnivores here. (B) contradicts the stated tendency. (E) is unsupported.

questions.stem: The author mentions the red deer of Jersey primarily in order to
choices: illustrate that body-size change on islands can occur quickly, suggesting strong selective pressure
provide an example of a lineage that does not follow the island rule
show that gigantism is more common than dwarfing among island deer
support the claim that the island rule is strongest on large islands
explain why predators were absent from Jersey
questions.explanation: Paragraph 3 begins "The changes can be fast" and says the Jersey deer shrank to a sixth of their mass in about six thousand years, "a pace implying strong selection." That is (A). (B) and (C) contradict the example, which is dwarfing consistent with the rule. (D) contradicts paragraph 4's "small, remote islands." (E) is not discussed.

questions.stem: The passage suggests that the third explanation described in the second paragraph differs from the other two in that it
choices: applies only to carnivores rather than to herbivores
has been confirmed by recent statistical surveys
attributes body-size change to the presence rather than the absence of predators
denies that islands have fewer competitors than the mainland
treats dwarfing and gigantism as outcomes of one process rather than responses to separate pressures
questions.explanation: The first two explanations address separate pressures: food limits for large animals, predator release for small ones. The third holds that species "converge on an intermediate body size," so that "dwarfing and gigantism are two expressions of a single tendency." That is (E). (B) is not stated; the surveys qualify the rule as a whole. (C) and (D) contradict the third account's "few competitors and few predators." (A) is unsupported.

title: Reconsidering First-Mover Advantage
paras: Business strategists have long held that the first firm to enter a new market enjoys durable advantages. Pioneers, the argument goes, can build brand recognition before rivals appear, reach efficient scale sooner, lock customers in through switching costs, and secure scarce inputs such as prime locations or key suppliers. Early empirical studies seemed to confirm the claim: in survey after survey, firms identified as market pioneers held substantially larger market shares than later entrants.

Those studies, however, drew their samples from firms that were still operating when the data were collected, and they often relied on managers' own recollections of who had entered first. Pioneers that had failed were thus largely invisible, and surviving early followers were sometimes recorded as pioneers. When researchers instead reconstructed the history of dozens of product categories from contemporaneous trade publications, a different picture emerged: nearly half of the true pioneers had failed outright, and the long-term leaders were more often firms that had entered several years after the first.

The lesson is not that moving first is a mistake but that its value is conditional. Where the underlying technology is stable and strong network effects bind users to whichever product they adopt first, an early lead can become self-reinforcing. Where technology is changing rapidly, the pioneer bears the costs of educating customers and discovering what they want, while followers can learn from its errors and enter with a better product.

questions.stem: According to the passage, the early empirical studies of first movers overstated pioneers' advantages partly because they
choices: relied on trade publications that exaggerated pioneers' market shares
examined only markets with strong network effects
measured market share over too short a period
excluded failed pioneers by sampling only surviving firms
classified all early entrants as followers rather than pioneers
questions.explanation: Paragraph 2 says the studies "drew their samples from firms that were still operating," so "Pioneers that had failed were thus largely invisible." That is (D). (A) reverses the role of trade publications, which were used in the corrective research. (E) reverses the misclassification: followers were sometimes recorded as pioneers. (B) and (C) are not mentioned.

questions.stem: The author would most likely expect a pioneer to retain long-term market leadership in which of the following situations?
choices: A new medical imaging technology whose design is improving rapidly and whose users can switch easily
A consumer electronics market in which customers do not yet understand what the product does
A market with mature, stable technology in which each user benefits from others using the same product
A market in which followers can observe the pioneer's mistakes and enter with a better product
A market in which the pioneer's managers have the clearest recollection of entering first
questions.explanation: Paragraph 3 says an early lead can become "self-reinforcing" where "the underlying technology is stable and strong network effects bind users." (C) meets both conditions. (A) and (D) describe the rapid-change setting that favors followers. (B) involves the pioneer bearing the "costs of educating customers." (E) is irrelevant to market outcomes.

questions.stem: The author's description of the research that relied on contemporaneous trade publications serves primarily to
choices: present evidence that undermines the conclusions of earlier studies
show that pioneers usually become long-term market leaders
explain why managers' recollections are generally reliable
argue that firms should never be the first to enter a market
illustrate how network effects bind users to early products
questions.explanation: Paragraph 2 says this reconstruction produced "a different picture": nearly half of true pioneers failed, and leaders were usually later entrants. It thus serves as evidence against the earlier studies, (A). (B) is what the reconstruction contradicts. (C) contradicts the criticism of recollections. (D) contradicts "not that moving first is a mistake." (E) belongs to paragraph 3.

title: Were Railroads Indispensable?
paras: Few propositions in American economic history once seemed more secure than the claim that the railroad was indispensable to the country's nineteenth-century growth. In 1964 the economist Robert Fogel challenged it with a deliberately provocative method. Rather than tallying the railroad's achievements, he asked how much worse off the economy would have been without it. He estimated the "social savings" of the railroad in 1890: the additional cost of moving the same agricultural freight by the best available alternatives, chiefly waterways and wagons, compared with the cost of moving it by rail. His figure was strikingly small, under 3 percent of gross national product.

Critics attacked the estimate from several directions. Some argued that the calculation was static, measuring a single year's transport bill while ignoring the railroad's dynamic effects: the demand it created for iron, coal, and machinery, the settlement patterns it encouraged, and the economies of scale it made possible for distant markets. Fogel replied that railroad demand had absorbed only a modest fraction of iron output, but the broader objection about long-run effects was harder to dispose of. Others questioned the realism of the alternative. Fogel's counterfactual economy relied partly on an expanded network of canals, but building that network would itself have required enormous investment, which a full accounting would have to charge against the savings that the alternative provided.

Later studies using detailed geographic data on how easily each county could reach markets have generally produced larger estimates than Fogel's, though still well short of the transformative role that older narratives assigned the railroad. These studies also suggest that the losses would have fallen unevenly, concentrated in regions far from navigable water, a distribution that a single national figure tends to obscure.

Whatever the correct figure, Fogel's lasting contribution lies less in his number than in his question. By forcing historians to specify the alternative against which an innovation should be judged, he replaced a debate about whether the railroad was indispensable, a question almost impossible to answer, with a debate about how much it mattered, which evidence can address.

questions.stem: Which of the following best describes the main point of the passage?
choices: Fogel's estimate of the railroad's social savings has been proven correct by later research.
The railroad was indispensable to American growth, as older narratives claimed.
Canals would have been a cheaper means of transport than railroads in the nineteenth century.
Fogel's estimate remains disputed, but his counterfactual method usefully reframed the debate over the railroad's importance.
Fogel's critics were mistaken to focus on the dynamic effects of railroads.
questions.explanation: Paragraphs 2 and 3 present objections and later estimates, and paragraph 4 says "Whatever the correct figure, Fogel's lasting contribution lies less in his number than in his question," which turned the debate toward "how much it mattered." That is (D). (A) contradicts the larger later estimates. (B) contradicts paragraph 3. (C) and (E) are not claimed.

questions.stem: According to the passage, Fogel's measure of the railroad's "social savings" was the
choices: total revenue earned by railroads in 1890
share of iron output absorbed by railroad construction
increase in gross national product that occurred after railroads were built
investment required to build a network of canals
additional cost of shipping the same agricultural freight by the best alternatives rather than by rail
questions.explanation: Paragraph 1 defines social savings as "the additional cost of moving the same agricultural freight by the best available alternatives, chiefly waterways and wagons, compared with the cost of moving it by rail." That is (E). (B) is Fogel's reply to critics, and (D) is a critics' point in paragraph 2. (A) and (C) are not his measure.

questions.stem: It can be inferred that critics who emphasized the railroad's demand for iron, coal, and machinery believed that Fogel's estimate
choices: overstated the railroad's importance by counting benefits to other industries
omitted gains that the railroad generated in industries supplying it
relied too heavily on the cost of building canals
measured transport costs in the wrong year
correctly captured the railroad's long-run effects
questions.explanation: Paragraph 2 says these critics viewed the calculation as "static," "ignoring the railroad's dynamic effects," including "the demand it created for iron, coal, and machinery." They thought the estimate left out such gains, so it understated the railroad's importance, (B). (A) reverses the direction. (E) contradicts the criticism. (C) and (D) are other objections or unsupported.

questions.stem: The objection concerning Fogel's network of canals implies that his estimate of social savings may have been too low because
choices: canals could carry more freight than railroads
Fogel overestimated how much iron the railroads used
the alternative economy would have produced more agricultural freight
wagons were more expensive than canals
the cost of building the alternative transport network was not fully counted
questions.explanation: Social savings equal the cost of the alternative minus the cost of rail. Paragraph 2 notes that building the canal network "would itself have required enormous investment," which a full accounting would charge against "the savings that the alternative provided." Counting that cost makes the alternative more expensive and the railroad's savings larger, so the estimate may have been too low, (E). (B) concerns another objection. (A), (C) and (D) are not claimed.

title: Which Came First?
paras: It is now widely accepted that mitochondria, the energy-producing structures of complex cells, descend from bacteria that once lived inside another cell. The question is what kind of cell that host was. On the traditional view, the host was already a sophisticated cell, equipped with a nucleus and an internal skeleton that allowed it to engulf other cells, and it acquired the future mitochondrion by swallowing it. A rival view reverses the order. It holds that the energy supplied by mitochondria was a precondition for complexity: a prokaryote, lacking internal power stations, can devote only a small energy budget to each of its genes, too little to sustain the large genomes and elaborate machinery of complex cells. On this account the host was a relatively simple archaeon, and the partnership began not as predation but as a metabolic exchange between neighbors.

The discovery of the Asgard archaea, the closest known prokaryotic relatives of complex cells, was expected to decide the matter. It has instead complicated it. Asgard genomes encode several proteins once thought unique to complex cells, including components of an internal skeleton, suggesting that the host was more elaborate than the simplest version of the rival view allows. Yet no Asgard cell has been observed engulfing another, and the cells studied so far are small and slow-growing. The host, it seems, was neither a simple prokaryote nor a fully formed complex cell. If modest internal complexity made the partnership possible and the partnership then made further complexity possible, the question of which came first may be less a puzzle awaiting a solution than a symptom of a poorly posed dichotomy.

questions.stem: According to the rival view described in the passage, prokaryotes could not by themselves become complex cells because
choices: they lacked the ability to engulf other cells
the energy available to support each of their genes was too small
they could not exchange metabolic products with neighboring cells
their genomes contained no proteins of an internal skeleton
they grew too slowly to compete with complex cells
questions.explanation: The rival view holds that "a prokaryote, lacking internal power stations, can devote only a small energy budget to each of its genes, too little to sustain the large genomes and elaborate machinery of complex cells." That is (B). (A) is part of the traditional view of the host. (C) contradicts the rival view's "metabolic exchange." (D) is undermined by the Asgard findings. (E) describes Asgard cells, not the rival argument.

questions.stem: The author's statement that the Asgard discovery has "complicated" the matter is best supported by which of the following observations in the passage?
choices: Asgard archaea are the closest known prokaryotic relatives of complex cells.
Mitochondria descend from bacteria that once lived inside another cell.
Asgard cells possess some features of complex cells but have not been observed engulfing other cells.
Asgard cells have been shown to contain mitochondria.
Asgard genomes are larger than those of most complex cells.
questions.explanation: The second paragraph explains the complication: Asgard genomes encode proteins "including components of an internal skeleton," which troubles the simplest rival view, "Yet no Asgard cell has been observed engulfing another," which troubles the traditional view. Evidence pulling against both is (C). (A) and (B) are background, not the complication. (D) and (E) are not stated.

questions.stem: The final sentence of the passage functions primarily to
choices: endorse the traditional view that the host cell engulfed the future mitochondrion
summarize evidence that the host was a simple prokaryote
predict that further study of Asgard archaea will settle the debate
dismiss the importance of the Asgard discovery
suggest that the debate may rest on a false choice between two strict orderings
questions.explanation: The last sentence proposes that complexity and the partnership may have reinforced each other, so asking "which came first" may reflect "a poorly posed dichotomy." That reframes the debate as a false choice, (E). (A) and (B) each take one side the sentence moves beyond. (C) contradicts the passage's claim that the discovery did not decide the matter. (D) ignores that the sentence builds on the Asgard evidence.

title: Why Firms Exist
paras: If markets allocate resources efficiently, why does so much economic activity take place inside firms, where managers issue commands rather than prices coordinating exchange? Ronald Coase's answer, offered in 1937, was that using the market is not free. Finding suppliers, negotiating terms, and enforcing agreements all impose costs, and a firm expands until the cost of organizing one more transaction internally equals the cost of conducting it through the market.

Oliver Williamson later specified when market transactions become especially costly. When one party must make investments tailored to a particular trading partner, such as a supplier that builds a plant beside a single customer's factory, each side becomes vulnerable to the other's opportunism. The customer can demand lower prices once the plant is built; the supplier can threaten to withhold output. Bringing both stages under common ownership removes the incentive for such hold-up. The textbook illustration is General Motors' acquisition of the auto body maker Fisher Body in the 1920s, though business historians have since questioned whether the hold-up problem in that case was as severe as the story requires.

A different tradition, the capabilities view, locates the reason for firms elsewhere. Firms exist, on this account, because they accumulate knowledge that is tacit, collective, and difficult to describe in a contract. A team that has learned over years how to make a complex process work cannot simply be rented by the hour. The boundaries of the firm reflect where such knowledge resides, not merely where exchange is hazardous.

The two accounts are often presented as rivals, but each answers a question the other neglects. Transaction cost reasoning explains why a firm might internalize an activity it could perform either way; the capabilities view explains which activities a firm can perform well at all. A firm may outsource a function despite a real risk of hold-up because it lacks the competence to do the work, or keep a function in-house despite an ample supply of reliable contractors because its know-how cannot be transferred. Transaction cost theorists have tended to treat what firms are able to do as given, and that assumption conceals much of what determines a firm's boundaries.

questions.stem: The primary purpose of the passage is to
choices: argue that the capabilities view has made transaction cost economics obsolete
explain how General Motors' acquisition of Fisher Body solved a hold-up problem
present two explanations for the existence of firms and argue that they complement each other
show that markets allocate resources more efficiently than firms do
describe the history of vertical integration in the automobile industry
questions.explanation: Paragraphs 1 and 2 present transaction cost reasoning, paragraph 3 the capabilities view, and paragraph 4 says "each answers a question the other neglects." That is (C). (A) overstates; the author keeps transaction cost reasoning. (B) and (E) are narrow details, and the Fisher Body case is even questioned. (D) is not argued.

questions.stem: The author's remark that business historians have questioned the severity of the hold-up problem in the Fisher Body case serves primarily to
choices: refute Williamson's account of when market transactions become costly
suggest that General Motors should not have acquired Fisher Body
show that the capabilities view better explains the Fisher Body acquisition
acknowledge that a famous illustration of a theory may be weaker than its prominence suggests
argue that hold-up problems never arise between suppliers and customers
questions.explanation: Paragraph 2 calls the case "the textbook illustration" and then adds that historians question "whether the hold-up problem in that case was as severe as the story requires." The remark casts doubt on the example, not the theory, which the author goes on to treat as valid in paragraph 4. That is (D). (A) and (E) overreach. (B) is not argued. (C) is never linked to Fisher Body.

questions.stem: Which of the following situations would be better explained by the capabilities view than by the transaction cost view, as the passage presents them?
choices: A manufacturer buys the sole supplier of a custom component after the supplier threatens to withhold output.
A retailer purchases standard shipping boxes from whichever of many vendors offers the lowest price.
A firm acquires a supplier whose plant was built beside the firm's factory to serve it alone.
A firm signs a long-term contract with a supplier to reduce the costs of renegotiating prices each year.
A firm keeps a specialized design team in-house although many reliable outside design firms are available, because the team's accumulated know-how cannot be transferred.
questions.explanation: Paragraph 4 says a firm may "keep a function in-house despite an ample supply of reliable contractors because its know-how cannot be transferred," a case transaction cost reasoning, focused on hazardous exchange, does not explain. (E) matches. (A) and (C) are hold-up situations explained by transaction costs. (B) and (D) are ordinary market contracting consistent with transaction cost logic.

questions.stem: The author implies that transaction cost economics is incomplete chiefly because it
choices: ignores the costs of negotiating and enforcing contracts
overstates the importance of opportunism between trading partners
relies on historical examples that cannot be verified
takes for granted which activities a firm is capable of performing
assumes that markets allocate resources perfectly
questions.explanation: The final sentence states: "Transaction cost theorists have tended to treat what firms are able to do as given, and that assumption conceals much of what determines a firm's boundaries." That is (D). (A) and (E) contradict Coase's central point that markets are costly. (B) is not criticized. (C) overgeneralizes from the Fisher Body remark.
